Its proposed score is "a two-feature logistic regression over u_ent(x) and u_pc(x)" — i.e., ENTROPY + a Probability-of-Correctness (PC) / correctness probe only. OVERREACH part: "no single signal reliably flags incorrect LLM outputs across tasks/models" overgeneralizes. The paper's negative claim is scoped specifically to entropy (a "model-dependent" failure in a "confidently wrong regime" of low-entropy hallucinations); it does not establish that every single signal fails. Also "substantially improves" overstates the paper's "generally improves."
correction: The high-level thesis and the evaluation-protocol description are correct, but the fusion recipe is wrong and must be corrected. The paper does NOT fuse "entropy + margin + semantic entropy + self-consistency." Its actual proposed gate is a two-feature logistic regression combining just two signals: token/sequence ENTROPY (u_ent) and a Probability-of-Correctness / correctness PROBE (u_pc). Semantic entropy (SE) and the semantic-entropy probe (SEP) are evaluated only as baselines, and margin / self-consistency are not used. Restate as: "the paper fuses entropy with a trained correctness (probability-of-correctness) probe." Also narrow "no single signal reliably flags incorrect outputs across tasks/models" to the paper's actual, entropy-specific finding (a model-dependent 'confidently-wrong' low-entropy failure mode), and soften "substantially improves" to "generally improves." evidence: Source opened and verified at the primary level (fetched abstract page, HTML, and downloaded the 765 KB PDF, then extracted its text). Paper confirmed: "Re-evaluating Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding for Automatic Speech Recognition," Yuu Jinnai, TMLR 05/2026, arXiv:2510.19471 — genuinely an ASR/ST paper using sample-based MBR decoding on Whisper. The load-bearing factual assertions in the claim are CONFIRMED verbatim from the Method section: "We use the BLEU score ... as the utility function of MBR. We do not use WER (CER) as the utility function because MBR decoding is known to inflate the score used as the utility function which may not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities (Freitag et al., 2022; Kovacs et al., 2024)." Corroborated by two table captions ("MBR using SentBERT may lead to inflate SemDist scores that do not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities"; Table 10: "BLEU scores are used as the utility function for MBR decoding, which may lead to artificially inflated scores that do not accurately reflect a model's true capabilities"). So: (a) the paper DOES deliberately avoid WER/CER as the utility, and (b) the stated reason IS that MBR inflates whatever score it optimizes. That much is exact. The claim is downgraded to PARTIAL only for its interpretive tail.
correction: Two nuances the claim overstates. (1) The paper does not present MBR utility inflation as its own finding — it states it as ESTABLISHED prior knowledge ("is known to inflate"), citing Freitag et al. 2022 and Kovacs et al. 2024. It is real and correctly cited, but this paper is a downstream user of the result, not its source. (2) More importantly, the framing "a concrete instance of the over-optimization edge that a budget/regularization constraint must bound" is the claimant's own theory-side extrapolation, NOT what the paper does. The paper's actual mitigation for the inflation is METRIC DECOUPLING — choosing a utility (BLEU) that differs from the evaluation metric (WER/CER) so the reported score is not the optimized score. It uses no budget cap or regularization/KL term to bound over-optimization; the N=64 sample count is a fixed compute setting justified nowhere as a convergence constraint. So the paper supports "the over-optimization/Goodhart edge is real," but it does NOT validate the specific remedy (budget N* / regularization β) the project's convergence-theory track invokes. Cite this paper as evidence the edge exists and that practitioners avoid optimizing the eval metric directly — not as evidence that a budget/regularization constraint is the mechanism that bounds it.

Opened arxiv 2502.18581 ("Scalable Best-of-N Selection... via Self-Certainty") via arxiv.org/html/2502.18581 plus corroborating searches. The claim's FRAMING is right but its DEFINING FORMULA is wrong.

CONFIRMED sub-claims:
- Training-free, gold-free, reward-model-free Best-of-N selector using only the model's own output distribution: paper states it estimates response quality "without requiring external reward models." 
- Rank N candidates, pick the max self-certainty (best-of-N).
- Cheap / effectively free at generation: "almost no computational overhead, as the token distribution is generated alongside the tokens during inference."

REFUTED — the core mathematical definition. The paper defines self-certainty as a KL-divergence-from-uniform DISTRIBUTIONAL measure that sums over the ENTIRE vocabulary V at every position: Self-Certainty = -(1/nV) Σ_{i=1..n} Σ_{j=1..V} log(V·p(j | x, y_<i)) (some renderings normalize by 1/n vs 1/nV, but both sum over all V). The claim instead defines it as the mean token log-probability SC(y)=(1/|y|)Σ log P(t_i|t_<i) — i.e., the log-prob of only the sampled tokens (perplexity/likelihood). That is a DIFFERENT quantity, and critically it is the exact BASELINE the paper argues against: the paper treats perplexity/mean-log-prob as a separate baseline and finds it substantially worse ("negative perplexity fails to clearly separate correct from incorrect outputs"; perplexity plateaus/declines after N≈16 while KL-based self-certainty keeps improving to N=64). So the claim mislabels the method as the very metric the paper shows is inferior.

Mean-log-prob / perplexity is a separate, weaker baseline the paper explicitly shows underperforms self-certainty. The specific 'P(True) self-evaluation is biased because models find their own content credible' framing is not verbatim in this paper but is (a) the standard self-preference-bias finding the source hint's 'self-verification/self-evaluation topic pages' cover, and (b) consistent with this paper's 'confidence tracks agreement, not truth' result. Primary source: 'Your Pre-trained LLM is Secretly an Unsupervised Confidence Calibrator', arXiv:2505.16690v2 (NeurIPS 2025). The load-bearing specific number is EXACT: in the experiment tables, Gemma-3-12B-Instruct on MMLU goes from Vanilla/uncalibrated ECE 23.679% -> DACA (unsupervised) 8.596%, versus supervised temperature scaling 9.746% — i.e. the unsupervised method not only 'reaches near labeled-TS quality' but slightly beats it (lower ECE). Same pattern holds across models (Llama-3-70B 7.844% vs 8.360% TS; Qwen3-8B 8.393% vs 8.655% TS); abstract headline is 'up to 15.08%' average ECE improvement. Textbook calibration facts in the claim (temperature scaling is 1-parameter and rank/order-preserving; isotonic is monotonic/piecewise-constant and needs more dev data; Platt) are standard and correct. NOTE for transparency: DACA's actual unsupervised mechanism is filtering to examples where the pre-trained and post-trained model AGREE and minimizing KL between their confidence distributions to fit tau — it is NOT literally 'self-consistency-based proxy targets from offline sampling' as the claim's general framing states, though it is a label-free/unsupervised proxy in the same spirit. The numeric and near-labeled-TS-quality claims are fully confirmed.

All three primary sources confirm the claim. SAFER (arXiv:2510.10193): 'a two-stage risk control framework comprising abstention-aware sampling and conformalized filtering'; it 'appl[ies] the conformal risk control method to determine a statistically valid uncertainty threshold, which filters unreliable distractors', and 'introduces an additional risk level ... thereby controlling the risk of correct answers being excluded' (= recall-floor / bounding probability of excluding a correct answer below a user-set level); uses Clopper-Pearson exact (finite-sample). Conformal Abstention (arXiv:2405.01563, 'Mitigating LLM Hallucinations via Conformal Abstention') establishes exactly two finite-sample guarantees: '(i) a participation guarantee ... and (ii) a conditional correctness guarantee' — matches the claim verbatim in substance. SCOPE (arXiv:2602.13110, ICML 2026, 'Selective Conformal Optimized Pairwise LLM Judging'): 'Under exchangeability, SCOPE calibrates an acceptance threshold such that the error rate among non-abstained judgments is at most a user-specified level alpha' (= any scoring function -> statistically valid accept/reject set via dev-set calibration). Distribution-free-under-exchangeability holds for all three (conformal).

All components verified. USC (arXiv:2311.17311, 'Universal Self-Consistency for LLM Generation'): 'leverages LLMs themselves to select the most consistent answer among multiple candidates', explicitly for free-form tasks where original SC's answer-extraction fails (code, summarization, open-ended QA). Fine-Grained/semantic SC (arXiv:2407.02056, ACL 2024): clusters/integrates segment-level commonalities across candidates for free-form generation. Self-certainty (arXiv:2502.18581, 'Scalable Best-of-N Selection ... via Self-Certainty'): the cheap logit-space variant — measures divergence of the predicted token distribution from uniform, using only the LLM's own logits, no reward model. Semantic entropy: original SE work (Kuhn et al. 2302.09664; Farquhar et al., Nature 2024) reports AUROC ~0.83 on TriviaQA and ~0.76 on clinical QA per the semantic-entropy topic literature (matches claimed 0.76-0.83); SE shows strong NEGATIVE correlation with accuracy and 'enables adaptive inference procedures such as early termination'/abstention (matches 'abstention/early-stop gating'). All specific numbers land in the stated range.

Mechanisms all verified. ROVER: builds a word confusion network from the 1-best hypotheses of the ASR systems then selects the best word in each bin via majority voting (matches claim; original author is J. Fiscus 1997, not 'Fischer' as the source hint spells it). Segment-level QE ranking: arXiv:1706.07238 'Automatic Quality Estimation for ASR System Combination' proposes exactly a ROVER variant that ranks transcriptions at segment level via QE instead of confidence scores. 'Diversity/complementarity provably drives WER reduction': supported by the theoretical-analysis literature (Audhkhasi et al., 'Theoretical Analysis of Diversity in an Ensemble of ASR Systems', TASLP 2014) which proves ROVER WER decomposes into average individual WER minus average WER w.r.t. the ROVER output — so complementary/diverse errors are provably the driver. ProGRes (arXiv:2409.00217): prompted generative rescoring that expands the n-best with LLM-generated hypotheses, combining ASR confidence + LLM sequence scoring + prompt-based expansion, reporting 5%-25% relative WER improvement (exact match to claim). GER 'better than any input hypothesis / beyond n-best oracle': confirmed by survey arXiv:2502.19548 and HyPoradise (2309.15701). CAVEAT: the specific '~14% WERR' figure for ROVER could not be located in the cited primary sources (plausible as a representative ROVER number but unsourced).

Primary source: 'AudioJudge: Understanding What Works in Large Audio Model Based Speech Evaluation', arXiv:2507.12705v1. CONFIRMED parts: pairwise > pointwise ('pairwise evaluation provides consistently more reliable results than pointwise evaluation', Appendix E); audio CONCATENATION of examples/ref+candidate improves performance ('audio concatenation combined with in-context learning significantly improves performance', e.g. TMHINTQ MSE 3.46->1.80, SOMOS 3.31->2.81); few-shot/in-context learning helps; up to 0.931 Spearman with human preferences (ChatbotArena-Spoken) / 0.912 (SpeakBench). OFF details: (1) the claimed '73-89% per-dimension accuracy' is CONTRADICTED — actual per-characteristic detection accuracies are lower: pronunciation 66.5%, speaking rate 55.3%, speaker ID 70.0%, speech-quality tasks 64.0-74.5% (human ceiling only 76.2%). (2) The '15-25% higher correlation with humans vs traditional metrics' figure is not substantiated by the paper's reported numbers (headline is up to ~0.91-0.93 Spearman). (3) 'Chain-of-thought before the verdict SIGNIFICANTLY raises human agreement' is not isolated/measured as a discrete ablation — reasoning is integrated into all prompt templates rather than tested as a variable.
correction: Accurate statement: AudioJudge finds pairwise > pointwise and that audio concatenation + in-context (few-shot) learning materially improve human-preference correlation (up to ~0.91-0.93 Spearman). Per-dimension audio-characteristic detection accuracy is ~55-74.5% (near the 76.2% human ceiling), NOT 73-89%. The 15-25%-higher-correlation and the CoT-'significantly raises agreement' claims are not established as reported/tested quantities in this paper.

support: Primary source: 'Attention in Large Language Models Yields Efficient Zero-Shot Re-Rankers' (ICR), arXiv:2410.02642 (ICLR 2025). CONFIRMED: ICR reads relevance off the change in the frozen LLM's attention pattern caused by the query; it needs 'two (O(1)) forward passes to re-rank N documents' (constant in N) and is 'substantially more efficient than generative re-ranking methods'; it outperforms RankGPT (and is 'specially strong on tasks that require more complex re-ranking signals') while reducing latency 60%+; because it requires the internal attention distribution it can only run on open models where attention weights are accessible (the claim's 'REQUIRES access to attention of all layers/heads' limitation is correct). OFF detail: the baseline complexity is misstated. The paper contrasts ICR's O(1) against generative/listwise rerankers needing 'at least O(N) forward passes' — NOT O(N log N) as the claim's parenthetical states.
correction: ICR is O(1) (exactly two forward passes, independent of N). The correct baseline comparison per the paper is O(N) forward passes for generative listwise rerankers (e.g., RankGPT), not O(N log N).

support: Primary sources: RankZephyr (arXiv:2312.02724) and RankVicuna (arXiv:2309.15088) are both zero-shot LISTWISE document rerankers that operate via prompting alone (no task-specific training on the target labels), reranking multiple candidates jointly to decide relative order. RankVicuna is 'the first fully open-source LLM capable of ... listwise reranking in a zero-shot setting', matching GPT-3.5-level effectiveness at 7B; RankZephyr 'bridges the effectiveness gap with GPT-4 and in some cases surpasses' it, and is 'resilient against variations in initial document ordering and the number of documents' — supporting the prompt/order-robustness point (the source hint's ECIR'25 Sun et al. prompt-variation study is corroborating secondary support, not individually re-verified here). Listwise > pointwise via jointly attending to multiple candidates is the established RankGPT ('Is ChatGPT Good at Search?') finding, and listwise reranking of retrieved passages is a standard training-free RAG-quality win. Core claim substantiated.

All parts verified. 'Increasing N worsens over-optimization' and 'pessimism (LCB) avoids collapse': arXiv:2604.04648 'From Curiosity to Caution: Mitigating Reward Hacking for Best-of-N with Pessimism' — BoN 'performance degrades as N increases due to selection of responses that exploit imperfections in the reward model', and their 'caution' method uses lower confidence bounds (LCBs) on value estimates / penalizes prediction error as distributional-uncertainty signal to down-weight atypical responses. HedgeTune/SBoN/Best-of-Poisson finding reward-KL-optimal stopping N*: arXiv:2506.19248 'Inference-Time Reward Hacking in LLMs' (NeurIPS 2025) — HedgeTune 'recovers the hacking threshold' and for BoN/BoP 'recovers the optimal number of samples n'; BoP is a 'near-exact approximation of the optimal reward-KL divergence policy'; SBoN smoothing 'mitigate[s] reward over-optimization'; the KL/regret smoothing lens is arXiv:2507.05913. MBR-regularized BoN bounding KL to the base policy: arXiv:2404.01054 'Regularized Best-of-N Sampling with Minimum Bayes Risk Objective' (NAACL 2025) — adds an MBR proximity regularizer to the reference/base policy (RBoN-KL and RBoN-WD variants) to mitigate reward hacking. Every mechanism in the claim maps to a real primary source.

THREE cited pillars all check out. (1) Model-Based MBR: 'Model-Based Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding for Text Generation' (Jinnai, Morimura, Honda, Ariu, Abe; arXiv:2311.05263v2, 12 Jun 2024). Abstract: 'MBR decoding selects a hypothesis from a pool of hypotheses that has the least expected risk under a probability model according to a given utility function' — i.e. maximizes expected utility scored against the candidate pool (verifier/reference-free, pool as pseudo-references). (2) Reranking-then-MBR beats vanilla MBR: 'Regularized Best-of-N Sampling with Minimum Bayes Risk Objective for LM Alignment' (Jinnai, Morimura, Ariu, Abe; arXiv:2404.01054v4, NAACL 2025) proposes MBR-BoN and shows it 'outperforms both BoN sampling and MBR decoding' on AlpacaFarm/hh-rlhf. (3) CBMBR: 'Centroid-Based Efficient Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding' (Deguchi et al., arXiv:2402.11197, ACL 2024 Findings) clusters pseudo-references and scores against centroids, cutting complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), 5.7x faster and up to +0.5 COMET on WMT'22/23.
correction: Minor framing note (not a defect): the 'utility can be embedding similarity or negative cross-WER' generalization is the standard MBR utility framework instantiated for speech; the two cited MBR papers demonstrate embedding/quality metrics (COMET/BLEU-family), not WER specifically. 'reranking-then-MBR' is realized in 2404.01054 as a joint MBR-regularized BoN objective rather than a strict rerank-then-MBR pipeline, but the direction (combining reward reranking with MBR >= vanilla MBR) is exactly what it shows.

support: 'CoCoA: Confidence and Context-Aware Adaptive Decoding for Resolving Knowledge Conflicts in LLMs' (Khandelwal, Gupta, Agrawal; arXiv:2508.17670v2, 25/27 Aug 2025; Accepted to EMNLP'25 Main). Full-text equations match the claim EXACTLY: Renyi divergence order alpha D^alpha_t(p_theta || p_theta^ctx) = 1/(alpha-1) log sum_i p_theta(y)^alpha p_theta^ctx(y)^(1-alpha) with alpha=0.5; entropy gap Delta-H_t = H(p_theta) - H(p_theta^ctx); contextual peakedness m_t = p_theta^ctx(y^(1)) - p_theta^ctx(y^(2)); conflict score s_t = sigma(D^alpha_t + gamma*Delta-H_t + delta); blend weight lambda_t = sigma(z log m_t + log((1-s_t)/s_t)) [= sigma(z log m_t + logit(1-s_t)) since logit(1-s)=log((1-s)/s)]; final q(y_t) proportional to p_theta^ctx(y_t)^lambda_t * p_theta(y_t)^(1-lambda_t). Fixed hyperparameters stated: alpha=0.5, z=5.0, gamma=1.0, delta=1e-8; 'we fix hyperparameters ... to ensure fair comparison' — no per-task training. Every element of the claim is verbatim-correct.

CoCoA (arXiv:2508.17670v2), Table 5 and surrounding text. NQ-SYNTH low-conflict: Greedy 88.20, CAD 64.00, CoCoA 86.60; paper states 'Unlike CAD, which showed a notable performance drop of 24.2 pts on NQ-SYNTH compared to greedy decoding, CoCoA maintained near-optimal accuracy' (88.2 - 64.0 = 24.2, matching the claimed ~24-pt collapse). NQ-SWAP high-conflict: CoCoA 80.80, and 'CoCoA achieved the highest accuracy on NQ-SWAP (80.8%), surpassing AdaCAD by 18.0 pts, COIECD by 30.0 pts, and greedy decoding by 29.2 pts.' All three numbers (86.6 / 64.0 / 88.2) and the +18.0-over-AdaCAD figure are exact. The kNN-Whisper OOD-harm / recall-floor linkage is the survey's own interpretive analogy, not a paper claim, and is not contradicted.

'Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Adaptive Test-Time Reasoning' (Nguyen, Gupta, Le, Deakin Univ.; arXiv:2605.26849v1, 26 May 2026). Correct in direction: it reallocates a FIXED total budget B=N*M from confident to uncertain questions and beats uniform at equal compute — GPQA (N=4, Qwen2.5-7B) UAB 35.6 vs Uniform 33.7 (+1.9); MATH500 UAB 69.9 vs Uniform 68.5 (+1.4); max +5.0 on Formal Logic (Qwen2.5-1.5B). It is training-free (Phase-1 log-probs only).
correction: Two specifics are wrong. (a) The per-question uncertainty signal is ANLL (average negative log-likelihood extracted from Phase-1 generations), NOT 'self-consistency variance.' (b) There is NO 'stopping when the hardest-easiest uncertainty gap falls below threshold' rule; allocation is a two-round concave-knapsack: Phase-1 gives every question one sample, then the remaining (N-1)M budget solves max sum_i [1-(1-p_i)^{N_i}] s.t. sum N_i = B via a marginal-greedy algorithm proven exact under KKT conditions (Appendix A.2). So 'greedy' is the knapsack solver, not a greedy reallocation-with-stopping heuristic.

support: 'UCCI: Calibrated Uncertainty for Cost-Optimal LLM Cascade Routing' (Varun Kotte; arXiv:2605.18796, submitted 11 May 2026; cs.LG/cs.CL). It 'maps token-level margin uncertainty to a per-query error probability via isotonic regression' fit on a held-out calibration set, then picks the escalation threshold by constrained cost minimization. The paper's stated insight matches the claim near-verbatim: 'A raw token-margin signal is weak when used directly, but after a small isotonic fit on a held-out calibration set it becomes a near-optimal routing score ... Most of the cascade engineering value comes from making the routing score probabilistic, not from hand-tuning the final threshold.' Theory: isotonic calibration achieves O(n^{-1/3}) ECE sample complexity; empirically cuts NER-workload inference cost 31% at micro-F1 0.91 while dropping ECE 0.12->0.03.

The general concept is sound and the RL-variant flag is correct: 'Learning Conformal Abstention Policies for Adaptive Risk Management in LLMs and VLMs' (Tayebati et al.; arXiv:2502.06884v1, 8 Feb 2025) explicitly 'integrat[es] reinforcement learning (RL) with CP to optimize abstention thresholds' — correctly classified as NOT training-free / comparison-class. SCOPE (arXiv:2602.13110, 'SCOPE: Selective Conformal Optimized Pairwise LLM Judging', Badshah/Emami/Sajjad, 13 Feb 2026) IS a genuine selective-conformal gate: it calibrates an acceptance threshold so 'the error rate among accepted judgments is at most a user-specified level alpha under exchangeability' with 'finite-sample validity ... on the non-abstained judgments.'
correction: PASC is mis-cited/mischaracterized. arXiv:2605.18812 is 'PASC: Pipeline-Aware Conformal Prediction with Joint Coverage Guarantees for Multi-Stage NLP and LLM Pipelines' (Kotte). It is NOT a selective-risk-among-answered abstention gate; it provides a finite-sample distribution-free guarantee that ALL K pipeline stages (e.g. NER->NED->typing) are simultaneously covered with prob >= 1-alpha by reducing joint coverage to one scalar conformal problem on the max nonconformity score (96.4% end-to-end coverage vs 93.4% Bonferroni). Also, SCOPE's guarantee is 'error <= alpha under exchangeability' (marginal), not the PAC-style 'probability 1-delta' the claim attributes to the family; the '1-delta' framing belongs to Learning-then-Test/conformal-risk-control, not to the two named papers.

support: 'SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval' (Zubkova, Park, Lee; arXiv:2501.04899, 9 Jan 2025; ICASSP 2025). Full text confirms it gates retrieval on SEMANTIC entropy: SE(x) ~ -|C|^{-1} sum_{i=1}^{|C|} log p(C_i | x), computed 'over meaning' after generating 10 high-temperature answers and using 'bidirectional entailment ... to detect varying forms of one meaning' (cluster generations by semantic equivalence). It explicitly separates lack-of-knowledge from phrasing uncertainty ('the lexical form does not really matter as long as the answer is correct. Semantic entropy supports ... when the model is confused by subtle lexical variations') and uses entropy thresholds to select 'no retrieval' / 'single-step retrieval' / 'multi-step retrieval' depth. Every element of the claim is supported.

'ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence' (Wu, Wu, Zou; arXiv:2404.10198v3, orig 16 Apr 2024, rev 7 Feb 2025). Confirmed finding that even GPT-4 overrides its own correct prior >60% of the time when given incorrect retrieved context (corroborated across sources; ClashEval reports weaker-prior items are more susceptible and quantifies both directions — adoption of incorrect context vs correction of incorrect prior with correct context, i.e. the bidirectional prior-biased/context-biased accounting). Follow-ups both verified: 'Three Regimes of Context-Parametric Conflict: A Predictive Framework and Empirical Validation' (arXiv:2605.11574) proposes a 3-regime predictive framework (Regime 1 evidence coherence / Regime 2 parametric certainty / Regime 3 task knowledge requirement), and 'Task Matters: Knowledge Requirements Shape LLM Responses to Context-Memory Conflict' (Sun, Bai, Dredze; arXiv:2506.06485) shows injection strategies 'help[] context-only tasks but harm[] those requiring parametric knowledge' — exactly a when-injection-helps-vs-harms framework.

'SeaKR: Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval for Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Generation' (Yao et al.; arXiv:2406.19215v1, 27 Jun 2024). Full text confirms all three internal-state functions: uncertainty is the determinant of the regularized Gram matrix of the EOS-token hidden states H_<EOS>^(l) sampled over k generations, extracted from the MIDDLE layer (l = L/2 = 16) — i.e. a Gram-matrix eigenvalue-based (det = product of eigenvalues) uncertainty of hidden layers. It (a) uses this internal-state uncertainty to decide when to retrieve, (b) 're-ranks [snippets] based on LLM's self-aware uncertainty to preserve the snippet that reduces their uncertainty to the utmost', and (c) 'choose[s] among different reasoning strategies' by uncertainty comparison. The paper part is fully confirmed.
correction: Caveat on scope, not a defect: the second half ('llama.cpp's llama-server does not expose per-token hidden states, making the internal-state family infeasible on the GGUF resident-server stack') is engineering stack-knowledge, not a claim from the SeaKR paper and thus outside primary-source verification. It is technically reasonable — llama.cpp's server exposes only pooled/sequence embeddings, not arbitrary per-layer per-token hidden states needed for the Gram-matrix estimator — but should be treated as an engineering assertion, not a paper-verified fact. Also note 'eigen-uncertainty' is the log-determinant (sum of log eigenvalues), equivalent to the paper's regularized-Gram-determinant formulation.

support: All four gates verified as primary sources. (1) CGES = 'CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Efficient and Accurate Self-Consistency', arXiv:2511.02603 (Aghazadeh et al., Nov 2025): forms Bayesian posteriors over candidate answers from scalar confidence signals and 'adaptively halts sampling once the posterior mass of a candidate exceeds a threshold' (~69% fewer calls, e.g. 16.0->4.9, within 0.06pp accuracy) — matches 'Bayesian posterior-mass halt'. (2) RASC = 'Reasoning Aware Self-Consistency', arXiv:2408.17017, NAACL 2025 (2025.naacl-long.184): quality-of-reasoning + answer-consistency scoring for criteria-based early stopping (~70% fewer samples) — matches 'quality+consistency NAACL2025'. (3) 'Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency for Efficient Sampling in LLM Reasoning', arXiv:2601.02970 — matches. (4) CITE = 'CITE: Anytime-Valid Statistical Inference in LLM Self-Consistency', arXiv:2605.05873 (Ota et al., May 2026): E-process/anytime-valid certification under arbitrary data-driven stopping — matches 'anytime-valid confidence sequences'. The load-bearing '~7.9x fewer samples at <0.1% accuracy loss for the original Adaptive-Consistency' is verified against the primary source 'Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs', arXiv:2305.11860, EMNLP 2023 (2023.emnlp-main.761): abstract states it 'reduces the sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%'. Minor framing note: these methods target self-consistency/majority-vote sampling; the claim's phrase 'halt best-of-N' is a reasonable generalization but the papers say self-consistency, not reward-model best-of-N.

Components verified. P(True) self-evaluation (model scores its own answer yes/no, normalized yes-prob = confidence, no dev labels) is the canonical Kadavath et al. 2022 'Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know' method; verbalized confidence is standard. The 2-sample fusion cite resolves to 'Two Samples Are Enough: Verbal Confidence Meets Self-Consistency in Reasoning LLMs' (OpenReview 66D3rZrNjV): systematic eval of six verbalized-confidence methods, self-consistency, and their hybrid (VCSC) across nine benchmarks / three LRMs, finding 'just two samples are enough to achieve strong and reliable confidence estimation' — matches 'Two Samples Are Enough'. The adoption-gap claim is supported by arXiv:2601.07767 'Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence?' (Wang et al., Jan 12 2026): finds a dissociation where models 'almost never abstain' and are not cost-aware even when abstention is optimal — i.e. confidence is not converted into an abstention policy. Minor note: 2601.07767 emphasizes the failure-to-abstain more than asserting models are well-calibrated, and 'the fusion closes that adoption gap' is the survey's own synthesis rather than a single paper's stated result.

The specific numbers trace to a primary source: 'RAG based Question-Answering for Contextual Response Prediction System', arXiv:2409.03708, which reports that for out-of-domain/off-topic queries 98.59% of retrieved articles scored below 0.7 cosine similarity, and 88.96% of articles for relevant/on-topic company-data questions scored above 0.7 — rounding to the claim's ~98.6% and ~89%, supporting a top-1 0.7-similarity inject/skip gate. Adaptive-k = 'Efficient Context Selection for Long-Context QA: No Tuning, No Iteration, Just Adaptive-k', arXiv:2506.08479: a single-pass method that 'adaptively selects the number of passages based on the distribution of the similarity scores', explicitly no fine-tuning and no iterative LLM calls (up to 10x fewer tokens) — matches 'choose HOW MANY chunks with no tuning and no iteration'.

Primary source: 'MCTS-RAG: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search', arXiv:2503.20757, EMNLP 2025 Findings (per the yale-nlp/MCTS-RAG README). It integrates retrieval strategically within the MCTS reasoning search rather than a single up-front retrieve-then-generate step (confirmed in abstract/README). The results text states verbatim: 'it achieves over 20% improvement with Llama 3.1-8B and 6% with Qwen2.5-7B on CWQA, roughly 15% and 10% gains on GPQA' — exactly matching the claim's '+20% (Llama-3.1-8B) / +6% (Qwen2.5-7B) on ComplexWebQA, ~15%/10% on GPQA'. (Underlying table values e.g. Llama CWQA MCTS-RAG 67.3 vs weaker baselines are consistent.)

Primary source: 'CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing', arXiv:2305.11738 (Gou et al., ICLR 2024). Abstract confirms LLMs validate/amend outputs by interacting with external tools (search engine for fact-checking, code interpreter for debugging), evaluated on free-form QA, math program synthesis, and toxicity reduction. The body reports (applied to ChatGPT) ~7.7 F1 improvement across three QA tasks and a 79.2% reduction in toxicity probability, matching '+7.7 F1 on open-domain QA, 79.2% toxicity reduction' (numbers corroborated across multiple sources; note they appear in the paper body, not the abstract). The companion 'without external feedback self-correction degrades reasoning' result is Huang et al. 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet', ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.01798) — a real ICLR-2024 finding. Minor caveat: that paper is by a separate group (Google DeepMind/UIUC), so 'companion' is loose, but the substantive characterization is accurate.

Primary source: 'Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models', arXiv:2408.00724 (Wu et al.). It introduces REBASE (REward BAlanced SEarch); node expansion width uses softmax-normalized PRM reward under a fixed total budget: Wj = Round(Bi * exp(R(nj)/Tb) / sum_k exp(R(nk)/Tb)), paired with weighted (majority) voting. Paper states 'REBASE consistently outperforms sampling and MCTS methods across all settings, models, and tasks' and that MCTS 'consumes substantially more resources'. Compute-optimality: 'scaling inference compute with inference strategies can be more computationally efficient than scaling model parameters'; smaller-model dominance confirmed (Llemma-7B + advanced inference 'consistently outperform the Llemma-34B model'). All sub-claims match.

Comparison-class members verified as RL-trained/training-based (correctly positioned against training-free candidates). rStar-Math, arXiv:2501.04519: policy SLM + process preference/reward model 'built from scratch and iteratively evolved' over 4 rounds of self-evolution via MCTS — matches 'trains policy+PRM via self-evolution'. DeepSearch, arXiv:2509.25454: 'embeds structured search into the training loop', RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) + MCTS in training — matches 'RLVR+MCTS'. TreeRL, arXiv:2506.11902: 'on-policy tree search for RL training' with intermediate supervision — matches 'on-policy tree-search RL'. Pairwise-RM / PairJudge RM, arXiv:2501.13007: constructs 'Pairwise-443K' (443K pairwise comparisons) and trains the RM by SFT — matches '443K-pair trained RM'. Search-R1/ReSearch/DeepResearcher are RL-trained search agents; GenPRM/R-PRM are trained process reward models; Inference-Aware Fine-Tuning for BoN (arXiv:2412.15287) is fine-tuning-based. The categorization is accurate.

Primary source: 'Rethinking On-policy Optimization for Query Augmentation', arXiv:2510.17139 (the OPQE paper). All three number pairs verified in its tables: evidence-seeking Hit@20 79.7 (prompting/SPQE) vs 79.8 (+7B RL); ad-hoc NDCG@10 56.6 vs 57.5; tool retrieval 34.5 (SPQE) vs 29.0 (RL, where RL degrades the dense retriever). The exact sentence is present: 'simple, training-free query augmentation often performs on par with, or even surpasses, more expensive RL-based counterparts.' Minor note: the paper expands SPQE as 'Simple Pseudo-document Query Expansion' (HyDE-style pseudo-document generation via prompting); the claim's parenthetical 'structured prompting' is a loose label for the same method — functionally correct and all load-bearing numbers match.

Primary source: 's3: You Don't Need That Much Data to Train a Search Agent via RL', arXiv:2505.14146, EMNLP 2025 (2025.emnlp-main.1095). CONFIRMED parts: s3 keeps the generator frozen and RL-trains only a 7B searcher (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) using the 'Gain Beyond RAG' reward (accuracy with searcher context minus naive top-k RAG accuracy); s3's average over the 6 general-QA datasets is 58.9; and Table 1 lists s3 = 2.4k training examples vs Search-R1 = 170k and DeepRetrieval-BM25 = 70k. NOT supported: the specific '+6.9pp (58.9 vs 52.0)' over IRCoT. support: Paper: 'Scalable Best-of-N Selection for Large Language Models via Self-Certainty' (Kang, Zhao, Song), arXiv:2502.18581 (v1 25 Feb 2025; v3 12 Dec 2025). Self-certainty is defined (Eq.) as Self-certainty = -(1/nV) Σ_{i=1..n} Σ_{j=1..V} log(V·p(j|x,y_<i)), i.e. the per-token KL divergence of the model's predicted token distribution from the uniform distribution, averaged over the n output tokens — exactly the 'KL divergence from uniform' the claim states. Paper: metric 'estimate[s] response quality without requiring external reward models' (reward-free), 'self-certainty scales effectively with increasing sample size N, akin to reward models,' and 'generalizes effectively to open-ended responses, where self-consistency is inapplicable' because self-consistency needs exact-match answer clustering. Minor wording note: the KL is aggregated across TOKENS within each output to score it; across the N samples the method then selects (argmax) or does self-certainty-weighted/Borda voting — so 'aggregated across samples' is the selection/voting step, not the per-output score. Primary-source anchor verified. Paper: 's3' (search-agent RL for RAG), arXiv:2505.14146. The Gain-Beyond-RAG reward is defined GBR(Q) = Acc(G(Q, D_s3), A) − Acc(G(Q, D_RAG), A) where A is the ground-truth answer — computing it requires gold accuracy on both the s3-retrieved and naive-RAG generations. It is a training-time reward used to train the searcher (they even precompute the baseline accuracy term and restrict training to examples where naive RAG is wrong), i.e. gold-dependent, offline-only — never a deployment-time signal. This matches the claim's carve-out.
